body_markdown:
Picture it: It's January 2027, the parking lot is iced over, and 14% of your leases expire this month. Nobody is touring, and your leasing team is staring at a vacancy report that only goes in one direction.


That pain was actually baked in a year ago. But the good news is that the leases you sign over the next few weeks will determine what 2027 looks like. Which means you can still fix it!


##


**What a Lease Expiration Curve Actually Is**


Your lease expiration curve is how many leases end each month. A healthy curve follows demand; for instance, more expirations land in late spring and summer, when renters are out hunting, and fewer land in the cold, quiet months.


An unhealthy curve has spikes:


-


Maybe a big lease-up pushed a wave of 12-month leases into the same winter month.


-


Maybe a few years of "just sign them for 12" slowly piled expirations into the wrong season.


Either way, spikes mean more turns at once, more vacancy days, and a leasing team that's either buried or bored.


##


**Why 2027 Is the Year to Get This Right**


The market is finally starting to shift. After a record supply wave, new deliveries are slowing, and


[many forecasters](https://www.multifamilyexecutive.com/index%2Ephp/business-finance/2026-sets-stage-multifamily-recovery-despite-class-c-demand-concerns) expect 2027 and 2028 to be stronger years for operators. Fewer brand-new buildings means less competition for your renters, and more pricing power when a unit does turn.


Meanwhile, residents are staying put.


[Renewals account for roughly 57% of all leasing activity](https://www.cbre.com/insights/books/us-real-estate-market-outlook-2026/multifamily) , and they've been outpacing new leases on rent growth. Some operators budgeting for 2027 are seeing


[renewal rates of 60 to 65%](https://www.multihousingnews.com/how-operators-are-rethinking-multifamily-budgets-for-2027/) , well above the usual 50 to 55% target.


Put those together, and the math is clear. When retention is high, every expiration you do have matters more. You want those turns hitting the market when demand is peaking, not when it's hibernating.


##


**Five Moves to Smooth Your Curve Before 2027**


1.


**Map it today:** Pull every lease expiration for 2027 by month and unit type. Set a target for each month based on your market's seasonality. Many operators cap winter months well below summer ones. Now you know exactly where the spikes are.


2.


**Use lease terms as your steering wheel:** Stop defaulting to 12 months. If a new lease signed in December would expire into an overloaded month, offer a 14-, 15-, or 16-month term instead. Short terms of 7 to 9 months work the other direction. Build term premiums into your pricing so the right choice is also the easy one.


3.


**Start renewals earlier:** Send renewal offers 90 to 120 days out for anyone expiring in a heavy month. Early conversations give you room to suggest a term that helps both of you, and residents appreciate not feeling rushed.


4.


**Treat your revenue management system like a teammate, not a boss:** Most platforms can weight pricing by expiration targets. Check that yours is actually doing it and that the targets reflect 2027's reality, not 2023's lease-up.


5.


**Staff for the curve you have while you build the one you want:** Fixing a curve takes a full lease cycle, and until then, some months will still be heavy. That's where flexible staffing shines. Bring in experienced leasing consultants for renewal pushes and peak traffic, and add make-ready techs when turns stack up, so your full-time team doesn't burn out.


##


**The Payoff**


A smooth curve pays off in more ways than one: steadier occupancy, fewer rushed turns, and real pricing power when the market hands it to you. It also gives you a calmer team. When leasing pros aren't whiplashed between chaos and crickets, they stay longer, and your residents feel the difference.


The best time to fix your 2027 curve was last year. The next best time? This week.
